title: edge-savings-architecture-evidence-log
content:
Purpose

This working log captures a compact set of evidence and messaging assets to justify the claim: 'Redwood delivers material per-request cost savings for latency-sensitive LLM features by combining smart routing, KV-prefix caching, and workload-aware batching.' Intended audience: GTM reps, solutions engineers, and product marketing preparing customer narratives and proof-of-value demos.

High-level messaging hypotheses (one-liners)
- Hypothesis A: For conversational UX with short to mid-length context (<= 1024 tokens), Redwood reduces effective per-response token cost by 25–45% versus unmanaged single-node hosted endpoints through automated prefix/KV caching + micro-batching.
- Hypothesis B: For bursty, low-latency workloads (p95 latency SLO <= 200ms), Redwood’s routing + tiny-queue batching retains latency while improving cost vs naive single-request serving.
- Hypothesis C: When customers allow lightweight quantized variants for background fallback, overall availability and $/request improves by an additional 10–20% without visible quality regressions in ~80% of sessions.

Summary of technical mechanisms that create the savings
- Prefix/KV caching: Cache the common conversation prefixes at token-level; skip re-computation for cached KV keys and only generate new suffix tokens. Typical win when >30% of requests share stable system or user prompt prefixes.
- Continuous micro-batching: Group sub-millisecond arrival windows into tiny batches (2–8 requests) to amortize attention kernel overhead with minimal queuing.
- Smart routing: Route requests to a) hot model variants on dedicated pools for latency-critical routes, b) cheaper quantized variants or cold pools for background tasks, with policy-based automatic fallback.
- Workload-aware kernel selection: Runtime selects int8/int4 kernels and sequence-length-optimized attention kernels to reduce GPU cycles on expected request distributions.

Concrete proof points (current internal data)
- Chat demo workload (baseline: competitor-A single-node hosted, 16 token prefixes common):
  - Avg request size: 280 tokens; shared prefix portion 22%
  - Baseline competitor-A: p95 = 290ms, $/response = $0.0142
  - Redwood (prefix cache + micro-batching): p95 = 210ms, $/response = $0.0101 (≈29% cost reduction)
- High-concurrency short-turn dialogue (500 RPS spike for 30s):
  - Baseline: tail latency spikes to p95 = 720ms, 99th = 1.6s, many dropped due to client timeouts
  - Redwood (burst smoothing + routing): p95 = 230ms, 99th = 420ms, no client-side errors; effective $/request down 33% due to micro-batching and fewer re-tries
- Background embed/summary pipeline (large context, batching-friendly):
  - Using dedicated cold pools with quantized model variants reduced $/unit embedding by 42% vs competitor-A pricing in our spot benchmark; average latency acceptable for async jobs (2–6s)

Benchmarks to validate (planned, owner: Eng Benchmarking + SEs)
- Workloads to run: short-chat (100–400 tokens), multi-turn dialog (average 6 messages, 150 tokens each), long generation (1000–4k tokens), burst RPS patterns (sawtooth, Poisson, sudden 10x spikes).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, per-response GPU token compute time, queuing delay, number of cached hits, batch sizes distribution, $/response using realistic cloud GPU cost model.
- Comparators: competitor-A (managed hosted), competitor-B (self-hosted open runtime), in-house naive single-pool configuration.
- Success thresholds for messaging: reproduce >=25% $/response improvement at p95 <= competitor baseline p95 + 30ms for short-chat; demonstrate stable tail behavior under bursts (p95 < 300ms for 90% of spike scenarios).

Experiment matrix (short form)
- Matrix axes: workload type × routing policy (latency-first vs cost-first) × cache enabled/disabled × model quantization level.
- Quick pilots: 3 customers (SaaS chat, conversational FAQ, content gen) will be offered a 2-week PoV with detailed telemetry; collect sample payloads for prefix analysis.

Scriptable proof snippets for SDR/AE demos (two-line snippets)
- “We typically cut the per-response compute cost by a third on chat-like workloads by skipping work on repeated system prompts; can I show you the live telemetry for your payloads?”
- “If you need consistent p95 under spiky traffic, we can put that route on a dedicated hot pool and still keep $/request below what you’re paying for unmanaged endpoints.”

Competitive differentiation notes (short)
- Competitor-A (hosted): Strong single-request latency but no integrated prefix-KV cache or routing policies. They rely on customers to manage ad-hoc batching or caching in-app. This increases app-side complexity and re-requests.
- Competitor-B (open runtime): Flexible and low-level optimizations possible, but requires non-trivial ops work (kernel tuning, autoscale smoothing). Redwood’s differentiator: shipping these optimizations as a policy layer with observability and low-friction toggles.
- Competitor-C (enterprise inference vendor): Offers quantization & batching but often as sell-side professional services; Redwood: self-serve Optimize suggestions + conservative defaults for safe quality-preserving savings.

Risk & quality guardrails (what to call out in customer conversations)
- Risk: Heavy quantization without evals can surface hallucinations for specific instruction-heavy prompts. Guardrail: surface recommended prompt sets and in-platform A/B evals before enabling aggressive quantization.
- Risk: Over-eager batching may add latency for ultra-low-latency paths. Guardrail: per-route policy can pin to latency-first pool; micro-batching only used when route SLOs allow.

Sample unit-econ calculation (explainable in 60s to a buyer)
- Assumptions: baseline model cost = $0.12 / 1M tokens of effective GPU time; average response = 300 tokens; shared prefix = 25% (75 tokens avoided on cache hit).
- Baseline per-response cost = 300 tokens × ($0.12 / 1,000,000) = $0.000036 ≈ $0.036 per 1,000 responses (math-friendly numbers for talks).
- Redwood with 25% prefix cache hit: billed tokens computed = 225 tokens average ⇒ $0.000027 per response ⇒ 25% saving. Add micro-batching gains (amortize fixed kernel overhead ~0.006 per response at low scale) to approach a 30–40% net saving in real runs.

Sales-ready objection responses (quick bullets)
- “We already use batching”: Great — we often find app-level batching is coarser. Redwood optimizes batching at the kernel/runtime layer and couples it with cache hits, so you get amortization + cache without changing app logic.
- “What about quality?”: We run per-route evals and rollouts, and default conservative quantization on background routes only. For critical routes we keep FP16 paths.

Open questions (for eng/product follow-up)
- What is a realistic distribution of prefix-hit rates across early customers? (SEs to collect sample conversation logs under NDA)
- How much tail latency does optimistic routing add for multi-region fallbacks? Need microbench of cross-region fallback cost with cold KV misses.
- Can we formalize a simple $/response calculator in Console that combines caching rate, average tokens, and batch-size distribution? (Product-ops item)

Next steps (owner + eta)
- SEs: Collect 3 anonymized sample workloads from pilot customers by 2025-03-11 (owner: Jonas McKenna).
- Eng Benchmarking: Run the 6-scenario matrix and produce reproducible notebooks + raw telemetry by 2025-03-21 (owner: Diego Ramos).
- PM/Product Marketing: Draft an internal one-pager with two field-ready scripts + two charts (p95 vs $/response) by 2025-03-28 (owner: Meera Singh).

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep language for external-facing assets concrete (percent savings, latency numbers) and always show the benchmark assumptions.
- Avoid absolute statements like “always cheaper” — prefer conditional claims with SLO/capacity caveats.
- Attach quick dashboard screenshot in PoV decks showing cached-hit-rate, batch-size histogram, and p95 timeline.

End of log entry.
